Committed Step of Glycolysis: PFK-1
The committed step of glycolysis is the reaction catalysed by phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1),
which converts fructose 6-phosphate to fructose 1,6-bisphosphate.

Why is PFK-1 the committed step?
1
PFK-1 converts fructose 6-phosphate
to fructose 1,6-bisphosphate.
2
This reaction is effectively irreversible
in the cell (large negative AG).
3
Fructose 1,6-bisphosphate is a
downstream intermediate in glycolysis

fructose 6-phosphate to enter the
pentose phosphate pathway.
4
Therefore, once glucose has passed
this step, it is committed to
glycolysis and cannot easily be diverted
to the pentose phosphate pathway.
What does this mean?
PFK-1 determines the metabolic fate of glucose:
continuation through glycolysis to pyruvate and ATP
production.
Regulation of PFK-1 therefore controls the overall
flux of glucose through glycolysis.
Key points
• The committed step of glycolysis is catalysed by PFK-1
(F6P → F1,6BP).
• It is the first step unique to glycolysis and occurs after the
branch point with the pentose phosphate pathway.
• Committed steps determine the metabolic fate of a substrate
but are not always the only sites of regulation.

In the previous lecture, we introduced metabolism as a network of coordinated pathways that allow cells to obtain, store, and use energy. Carbohydrates, fats, and proteins can all contribute to ATP production, and their breakdown products eventually enter common metabolic pathways such as glycolysis, the TCA cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation.
In this lecture, we focus on glycolysis, one of the central pathways of carbohydrate metabolism.
Glycolysis converts:
Glucose to Pyruvate
through a sequence of 10 reactions in the cytosol.
During glycolysis, some of the energy stored in glucose is captured in two important forms:
ATP, which can be used directly by the cell
NADH, which carries high-energy electrons
Glycolysis is important because it occurs in the cytosol and is present in essentially all cells. It can produce ATP directly by substrate-level phosphorylation, without requiring the mitochondrial electron transport chain.
The pyruvate produced by glycolysis can then enter other pathways. Depending on the cell type and metabolic conditions, pyruvate may enter mitochondrial metabolism, for example the TCA cycle after conversion to acetyl-CoA, or it may be converted to lactate.
Key point: Glycolysis is a useful model for understanding three major ideas in metabolism: pathway organization, energy capture, and metabolic regulation.

Student Notes: How Does Glucose Enter Cells?
Glucose is water soluble, so it cannot freely diffuse through the hydrophobic lipid bilayer of the plasma membrane. Cells therefore need specific membrane transport proteins to move glucose across the membrane.
In most tissues, glucose enters cells through GLUT transporters. GLUT proteins are facilitated-diffusion transporters. They move glucose down its concentration gradient, from an area of higher glucose concentration to an area of lower concentration.
Because this is facilitated diffusion, GLUT-mediated transport does not directly require ATP. Different tissues express different GLUT isoforms, which allows glucose uptake to be matched to the metabolic needs of each tissue.
A major exception is the sodium-glucose cotransporter, SGLT. SGLT transports glucose together with Na⁺ into the cell. This is a form of secondary active transport.
SGLT does not hydrolyze ATP directly. Instead, it uses the energy stored in the Na⁺ gradient. That Na⁺ gradient is maintained by the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, which does use ATP.
SGLT transport is particularly important in:
the small intestine, for absorption of dietary glucose
the renal tubules, for reabsorption of filtered glucose
Key distinction:GLUT = facilitated diffusion, no direct ATP requirementSGLT = Na⁺-dependent secondary active transport
Take-home message: Different tissues use different glucose transporters, allowing glucose uptake to match tissue function and metabolic demand.

Glucose enters most cells through GLUT transporters, which mediate facilitated diffusion. Different tissues express different GLUT isoforms, allowing glucose uptake to match tissue function. 
GLUT1 is expressed in RBCs and many tissues. It has a low K_m, meaning high affinity for glucose, so it supports basal glucose uptake even when blood glucose is relatively low. 
GLUT2 is expressed in the liver, intestine, and pancreatic β-cells. It has a high K_m and high Vmax, so it has lower affinity but a high maximal transport rate. In the liver, it permits bidirectional glucose transport; in pancreatic β-cells it contributes to glucose sensing. 
GLUT3 is the major neuronal glucose transporter. Its very low Km gives it very high affinity, supporting continuous glucose uptake by the brain. 
GLUT4 is expressed mainly in skeletal muscle, adipose tissue, and heart. Insulin increases glucose uptake by promoting GLUT4 translocation to the plasma membrane; exercise can also stimulate GLUT4 translocation independently of insulin. 
Key concepts:Low K_m= high affinity.High Vmax = high maximal transport capacity.

GLUT4 is the major insulin-responsive glucose transporter in skeletal muscle, adipose tissue, and heart. 
In the fasting state, when insulin levels are low, most GLUT4 transporters are stored inside the cell in intracellular vesicles. Therefore, relatively few GLUT4 transporters are present in the plasma membrane and glucose uptake is lower. 
After a meal, insulin levels rise. Insulin signaling causes GLUT4-containing vesicles to move to and fuse with the plasma membrane. This increases the number of GLUT4 transporters at the cell surface and therefore increases glucose uptake. 
Exercise and muscle contraction can also stimulate GLUT4 translocation independently of insulin, which helps skeletal muscle increase glucose uptake during activity. 
In insulin resistance, GLUT4 translocation is impaired, reducing glucose disposal by skeletal muscle and adipose tissue. 
Key point: Insulin does not simply “open” GLUT4. It increases the number of GLUT4 transporters in the plasma membrane.

The liver plays a central role in maintaining whole-body glucose homeostasis.
 It can take up, store, produce, and release glucose depending on the nutritional state. 
In the fed state, glucose absorbed from the intestine reaches the liver through the portal circulation. The liver takes up glucose, stores excess glucose as glycogen, and uses some glucose through glycolysis. 
During fasting, the liver helps maintain blood glucose by breaking down glycogen through glycogenolysis and producing new glucose through gluconeogenesis from substrates such as lactate, glycerol, and amino acids. 
This glucose can then be released into the circulation to support tissues that depend heavily on glucose, particularly the brain and RBCs. 
Key point: The liver functions as a metabolic buffer, storing glucose when it is abundant and supplying glucose when dietary intake falls.

Glycolysis is the first major pathway of glucose metabolism. It consists of 10 enzyme-catalyzed reactions that occur in the cytosol. 
One molecule of glucose contains six carbons. Glycolysis converts it into two molecules of pyruvate, each containing three carbons.
The pathway can be divided conceptually into two parts:
Energy investment phase:The cell uses 2 ATP during the early reactions.
Energy payoff phase:Later reactions produce 4 ATP and 2 NADH.
Therefore, the net gain per glucose molecule is:
2ATP +2 NADH+ 2 pyruvate 
Glycolysis can generate ATP without directly consuming oxygen. This becomes especially important in cells such as RBCs and under conditions where oxygen availability is limited, which we will discuss later. 
Three glycolytic reactions are effectively irreversible under cellular conditions. They are catalyzed by:
Hexokinase or glucokinase
PFK-1
Pyruvate kinase 
Key point: Glycolysis begins with glucose and ends with pyruvate, while generating a small amount of ATP directly and producing NADH for further energy metabolism.

Glycolysis can be divided into two functional phases. 
The energy investment phase includes steps 1 to 5. During this phase, the cell uses 2 ATP to phosphorylate glucose and its intermediates. The six-carbon sugar is then cleaved into two three-carbon molecules.
The energy payoff phase includes steps 6 to 10. Because there are now two three-carbon intermediates, the reactions in this phase occur twice per glucose molecule. This phase produces a total of 4 ATP and 2 NADH, while forming 2 pyruvate.
The ATP balance is:
4 ATP produced - 2ATP consumed = 2ATP net
Key point: The first half of glycolysis prepares and splits glucose; the second half captures energy as ATP and NADH.

Glycolysis consists of 10 enzyme-catalyzed reactions. The first five reactions form the energy investment phase, while the last five form the energy payoff phase. 
ATP is consumed at:
Step 1, hexokinase/glucokinase
Step 3, PFK-1
At Step 4, aldolase cleaves the six-carbon fructose-1,6-bisphosphate into two different three-carbon molecules, glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate and dihydroxyacetone phosphate. DHAP cannot proceed directly through the remaining glycolytic reactions, so at Step 5, triose phosphate isomerase converts DHAP into G3P. Therefore, two G3P molecules continue through Steps 6–10 for every glucose molecule.
The three effectively irreversible reactions are:
Step 1: hexokinase/glucokinase
Step 3: PFK-1
Step 10: pyruvate kinase 
ATP is produced at:
Step 7, phosphoglycerate kinase
Step 10, pyruvate kinase

Key point: These three irreversible steps are the major control points of glycolysis, but PFK-1 is the committed step of the pathway.

Hexokinase catalyzes the first reaction of glycolysis:
Glucose +ATP → Glucose-6-phosphate +ADP
The reaction is effectively irreversible under cellular conditions and consumes one ATP. 
The main purpose of this reaction is to trap glucose inside the cell. Once glucose is phosphorylated to glucose-6-phosphate, it carries a negative charge and cannot leave through GLUT transporters. 
Hexokinase has a low K_m meaning high affinity for glucose, and a relatively low Vmax. This allows it to phosphorylate glucose efficiently even when glucose concentrations are relatively low. 
Hexokinase is inhibited by its product, glucose-6-phosphate, providing feedback regulation. 
Importantly, this is not the committed step of glycolysis, because glucose-6-phosphate can still enter other metabolic pathways.
Key point: Step 1 traps glucose inside the cell but does not yet commit it specifically to glycolysis.

Glucokinase catalyzes the same reaction as hexokinase:
Glucose +ATP → Glucose-6-phosphate +ADP
However, glucokinase is found mainly in the liver and pancreatic beta cells and has different kinetic and regulatory properties. 
Glucokinase has a high K_m, meaning lower affinity for glucose, and a high Vmax meaning it can process glucose at a high maximal rate when glucose concentration is elevated. This makes it well suited to handling the large rise in glucose after a meal. 
Unlike hexokinase, glucokinase is not inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate. In the liver, its expression is increased by insulin after meals. 
In the liver, glucokinase helps direct excess glucose toward glycogen synthesis and glycolysis, contributing to blood glucose buffering. In pancreatic beta cells, glucokinase contributes to glucose sensing and therefore helps couple rising glucose levels to insulin secretion. 
Mutations in the GCK gene can cause MODY2, which is associated with mild, stable fasting hyperglycemia. 
Key point: Hexokinase is suited to continuous glucose use at low concentrations, while glucokinase is suited to handling glucose when concentrations are high.

Hexokinase and glucokinase catalyze the same reaction, conversion of glucose to glucose-6-phosphate, but they differ in tissue distribution, kinetics, and regulation. 
Hexokinase is present in most tissues. It has a low K_m, meaning high affinity for glucose, and a low Vmax. This allows it to phosphorylate glucose efficiently even when glucose concentrations are relatively low. It is inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate. 
Glucokinase is found mainly in the liver and pancreatic β-cells. It has a high K_m and high Vmax. so it is most active when glucose is abundant, such as after a meal. It is not inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate, and its expression in liver is increased by insulin. 
Key point:Hexokinase supports continuous glucose use; glucokinase helps the liver and β-cells respond to high glucose concentrations.

PFK-1 catalyzes Step 3 of glycolysis:
Fructose-6-phosphate+ATP →Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate+ADP
This reaction is effectively irreversible under cellular conditions and is the committed step of glycolysis. 
It is called the committed step because metabolites before this reaction can still be diverted into other metabolic pathways. Once fructose-6-phosphate is converted to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate, the metabolite is directed forward through glycolysis.
PFK-1 is strongly regulated by the energy status of the cell.
AMP activates PFK-1, signaling that cellular energy is low and ATP production is needed.
ATP inhibits PFK-1, signaling that cellular energy is already sufficient.
Citrate also inhibits PFK-1, High citrate signals that downstream energy metabolism is well supplied, so glycolysis can be reduced.
Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate activates PFK-1, especially in the liver. 
Key point: PFK-1 integrates energy signals and determines whether glucose continues through glycolysis.

In the liver, insulin and glucagon regulate glycolysis indirectly through the bifunctional enzyme PFK-2/FBPase-2. phosphofructokinase-2 / fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase-2
In the fed state, insulin is high. This favors dephosphorylation of PFK-2/FBPase-2, making the PFK-2 domain active. 
PFK-2 produces fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, which strongly activates PFK-1. As a result, glycolysis increases. 
Insulin  → PFK-2 active → F2,6-BP ↑ →PFK-1 ↑  → Glycolysis  ↑
During fasting, glucagon increases cAMP and activates PKA. PKA phosphorylates PFK-2/FBPase-2. In the liver isoform, this makes the FBPase-2 domain active and PFK-2 inactive. 
F2,6-BP therefore falls, PFK-1 activity decreases, and glycolysis is suppressed. 
Glucagon → PKA →FBPase-2 active →F2,6-BP ↓ →PFK-1 ↓→Glycolysis↓
Key point: PFK-1 is controlled hormonally indirectly, through changes in fructose-2,6-bisphosphate.

Glucose enters cells mainly through GLUT transporters. In skeletal muscle and adipose tissue, insulin increases glucose uptake by promoting GLUT4 translocation to the plasma membrane. 15. Glycolysis I
Once inside the cell, glucose is phosphorylated to glucose-6-phosphate. Hexokinase functions efficiently at relatively low glucose concentrations, whereas glucokinase is adapted to handle high glucose concentrations, particularly in the liver after a meal. 15. Glycolysis I
The first five reactions of glycolysis form the energy investment phase. Two ATP are consumed, and one six-carbon glucose ultimately produces two molecules of glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate.
The major regulatory point is PFK-1, which catalyzes the committed step of glycolysis. PFK-1 responds to cellular energy status and, in the liver, is also regulated indirectly by insulin and glucagon through fructose-2,6-bisphosphate. 
Key transition: In Glycolysis II, both G3P molecules proceed through the payoff phase, where ATP and NADH are generated.

Entering the Payoff Phase
At the end of the energy investment phase, one glucose molecule has been converted into two molecules of glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, G3P.
From this point onward, each reaction occurs twice for every glucose molecule.
The payoff phase includes Steps 6 to 10. During these reactions:
2 NADH are produced
4 ATP are produced
2 pyruvate are formed
Because 2 ATP were consumed earlier in glycolysis, the overall net ATP gain is:
4-2=2ATP per glucose 
The first reaction we will examine is Step 6, where G3P is oxidized and NAD⁺ is reduced to NADH.

Step 6 is catalyzed by glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, GAPDH. It converts G3P to 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate. 
During this reaction, G3P is oxidized and NAD⁺ accepts electrons, becoming NADH. Inorganic phosphate is also incorporated into the molecule.
The product, 1,3-BPG, contains a high-energy phosphate bond. The energy stored in this intermediate will be used in the next reaction to generate ATP.
Because glycolysis produces two G3P molecules from each glucose, Step 6 occurs twice:
2 NAD+  → 2NADH
So glycolysis produces 2 NADH per glucose at this step.
Key point: Glycolysis depends on a continuing supply of NAD⁺. If NAD⁺ is not regenerated, Step 6 stops and glycolysis cannot continue

Step 7 is catalyzed by phosphoglycerate kinase.
1,3-BPG+ADP →3-phosphoglycerate+ATP
In this reaction, the high-energy phosphate group of 1,3-BPG is transferred directly to ADP, forming ATP. 
This mechanism is called substrate-level phosphorylation because ATP is formed by direct phosphate transfer from a metabolic intermediate to ADP.
Because there are two molecules of 1,3-BPG for every glucose molecule, this reaction produces: 2 ATP per glucose 
These 2 ATP effectively recover the 2 ATP that were consumed during the investment phase.
In RBCs, some 1,3-BPG can be diverted into the 2,3-BPG shunt, which influences hemoglobin oxygen affinity. 
Key point: Step 7 is the first ATP-producing reaction of glycolysis and the first example of substrate-level phosphorylation.

Step 8 is catalyzed by phosphoglycerate mutase. It converts 3-phosphoglycerate into 2-phosphoglycerate by moving the phosphate group within the molecule. Step 9 is catalyzed by enolase. Enolase removes water from 2-phosphoglycerate, producing phosphoenolpyruvate, PEP. 
PEP is a high-energy phosphate-containing intermediate. Its phosphate group will be transferred to ADP in Step 10 to generate ATP.
Key point: Steps 8 and 9 do not produce ATP directly. They prepare a high-energy substrate, PEP, for ATP generation in the next reaction.

Enolase catalyzes Step 9 of glycolysis, converting 2-phosphoglycerate to phosphoenolpyruvate.
Fluoride can inhibit enolase by interfering with the Mg²⁺-dependent active site of the enzyme. 
In oral bacteria, inhibition of enolase slows glycolysis and therefore reduces production of acidic end products such as lactate.
Less acid production means less acid-mediated demineralization of tooth enamel.
.

Pyruvate kinase catalyzes the final reaction of glycolysis:
PEP+ADP → pyruvate+ATP
PEP donates a high-energy phosphate group directly to ADP, producing ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation. Because there are two PEP molecules per glucose, Step 10 produces 2 ATP per glucose.
Pyruvate kinase is activated by fructose-1,6-bisphosphate, which provides feed-forward regulation. It is inhibited by ATP, signaling that cellular energy is already sufficient. 
In the liver, pyruvate kinase is also hormonally regulated. Glucagon promotes phosphorylation and decreases enzyme activity during fasting, whereas insulin favors dephosphorylation and increased activity in the fed state. 
Key point: Step 10 is the second ATP-generating reaction and the final effectively irreversible step of glycolysis.

Glycolysis contains three effectively irreversible reactions that act as major control points:
Step 1: hexokinase or glucokinaseStep 3: PFK-1Step 10: pyruvate kinase. 
Step 1 traps glucose inside the cell as glucose-6-phosphate. Hexokinase is inhibited by G6P, whereas glucokinase in the liver is adapted to handle high glucose concentrations.
Step 3, catalyzed by PFK-1, is the committed step of glycolysis. It is activated by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate and inhibited by ATP and citrate. 
Step 10, catalyzed by pyruvate kinase, generates ATP and pyruvate. It is activated by fructose-1,6-bisphosphate and inhibited by ATP. In the liver, it is also regulated by phosphorylation. 
Key point: All three are important control points, but PFK-1 is the committed step and the central regulator of glycolytic flux.

Pyruvate kinase deficiency is an inherited red-cell enzymopathy caused by pathogenic variants in PKLR.
PKLR is the gene that encodes the red blood cell/liver isoform of pyruvate kinase.
 Mature erythrocytes lack mitochondria and therefore depend heavily on glycolysis to generate ATP. When pyruvate kinase activity is reduced, ATP production falls, impairing membrane function and contributing to cellular dehydration and premature destruction of red cells. 
The disorder therefore produces chronic hemolytic anemia. Upstream glycolytic intermediates, particularly 2,3-BPG, may increase. Increased 2,3-BPG decreases hemoglobin's oxygen affinity and shifts the oxygen-dissociation curve to the right, which can improve oxygen delivery and partly explain why some patients tolerate their anemia better than the hemoglobin concentration alone might suggest. 
Key point: RBCs are especially vulnerable because they cannot compensate for impaired glycolytic ATP production using mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation.

Glycolysis itself does not directly consume oxygen. However, Step 6 requires NAD⁺, so glycolysis cannot continue unless NAD⁺ is regenerated. 
When mitochondrial oxidative metabolism is functioning, cytosolic NADH can ultimately be reoxidized and NAD⁺ regenerated through mitochondrial pathways.
When mitochondrial oxidation cannot keep pace with glycolysis, pyruvate can be reduced to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase:
Pyruvate+ NADH+ H+ ↔  Lactate+ NAD+ 
The critical purpose of this reaction for glycolysis is the regeneration of NAD⁺.
Mature RBCs are a special case because they lack mitochondria, so pyruvate is converted to lactate even when oxygen is available.

Pyruvate is the final product of glycolysis, but it is not necessarily the final metabolic product.
Its fate depends on the metabolic state and tissue:
Pyruvate can be reduced to lactate, regenerating NAD⁺.
It can be converted to acetyl-CoA by pyruvate dehydrogenase and enter mitochondrial oxidative metabolism.
It can be carboxylated to oxaloacetate, particularly when carbon is needed for gluconeogenesis or anaplerosis.
It can undergo transamination to form alanine. 
Key point: Pyruvate is a major metabolic branch point, not simply an end product.

Lactate formation is particularly important whenever cells need to regenerate cytosolic NAD⁺ rapidly.
Mature RBCs lack mitochondria, so they depend on glycolysis for ATP and routinely convert pyruvate to lactate
During intense exercise, lactate production rises because glycolytic production of pyruvate and NADH can exceed the rate at which mitochondrial oxidative metabolism can process them. Therefore, describing lactate production simply as a consequence of “no oxygen” is too simplistic.
Lactate is also not merely a metabolic waste product. It can circulate between tissues and be oxidized as fuel or used as a precursor for hepatic gluconeogenesis. 
Key point: lactate formation helps maintain NAD⁺ availability, allowing glycolysis to continue.

Blood lactate rises when lactate production exceeds its use and clearance.
This may occur with tissue hypoxia or poor perfusion, but lactate can also rise during intense exercise, seizures, or when clearance is impaired, particularly in liver dysfunction.
Hyperlactatemia simply means elevated blood lactate. Lactic acidosis refers to elevated lactate occurring together with metabolic acidosis.
The key clinical point is that an elevated lactate is not specific for tissue hypoxia and should always be interpreted in context.

The payoff phase begins with two molecules of G3P per glucose. Step 6 generates 2 NADH, while Steps 7 and 10 together generate 4 ATP, giving a net glycolytic gain of 2 ATP per glucose after the two ATP invested earlier.
Glycolysis also requires continuous regeneration of NAD⁺, because NAD⁺ is needed at Step 6. Lactate formation is one mechanism that regenerates NAD⁺.
Pyruvate is not simply an end product. It links glycolysis with lactate metabolism, mitochondrial oxidation, gluconeogenesis, and amino-acid metabolism.
Clinically, impaired pyruvate kinase activity is especially important in RBCs because mature RBCs depend on glycolysis for ATP. Elevated blood lactate should also be interpreted in context rather than assumed to indicate tissue hypoxia automatically.
Key point: Glycolysis is not just a sequence of ten reactions; it is a regulated pathway connecting energy production, redox balance, and multiple metabolic fates.

The lecture begins with the transition from pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, which links glycolysis to mitochondrial oxidative metabolism.
We will then follow acetyl-CoA through the TCA cycle, focusing on where carbon is lost as CO₂ and where energy is captured as NADH, FADH₂, and GTP.
The cycle is highly regulated according to the energy state of the cell. High ATP and NADH generally suppress pathway activity, while low-energy signals such as ADP and Ca²⁺ can stimulate key regulatory enzymes. 
The TCA cycle also has an important biosynthetic role. Intermediates can leave the cycle and contribute to synthesis of fatty acids, amino acids, heme, and glucose-related pathways. Because the cycle participates in both breakdown and synthesis, it is described as amphibolic
Finally, when TCA intermediates are withdrawn for biosynthesis, they must be replenished. This is the role of anaplerotic reactions, especially the conversion of pyruvate to oxaloacetate by pyruvate carboxylase.

Glycolysis ends in the cytosol with formation of pyruvate. For pyruvate to contribute to mitochondrial oxidative metabolism, it must first be converted into acetyl-CoA.
This reaction is catalyzed by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, PDH, in the mitochondrial matrix. During the reaction, one carbon is released as CO₂, and NAD⁺ is reduced to NADH.
The acetyl-CoA produced then enters the TCA cycle, where its two-carbon acetyl group is oxidized further. The cycle captures energy mainly in the form of NADH and FADH₂, which later contribute to ATP production through oxidative phosphorylation.
Key point: Glycolysis and the TCA cycle are linked by the conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA.

Pyruvate is produced in the cytosol, but both pyruvate dehydrogenase and pyruvate carboxylase are located in the mitochondrial matrix.
The outer mitochondrial membrane is relatively permeable to small metabolites through porins. The inner mitochondrial membrane is much more selective.
Pyruvate therefore crosses the inner membrane through the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier, MPC.
Once inside the matrix, pyruvate has two important metabolic fates that we will use in this lecture:
PyruvateAcetyl-CoA
through the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, linking glycolysis to the TCA cycle;
and
Pyruvate Oxaloacetate
through pyruvate carboxylase, which is important for anaplerosis and gluconeogenesis.
Key point: pyruvate cannot simply diffuse across the inner mitochondrial membrane; transport through MPC is required

The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex connects cytosolic glycolysis with mitochondrial acetyl-CoA metabolism.
Pyruvate contains three carbons. During the PDH reaction, one carbon is removed as CO₂. The remaining two-carbon fragment is oxidized and transferred to coenzyme A, producing acetyl-CoA.
At the same time, NAD⁺ accepts electrons and is reduced to NADH.
The reaction is therefore an oxidative decarboxylation:
decarboxylation because CO₂ is removed
oxidation because electrons are removed from the pyruvate-derived carbon fragment
PDH is an effectively irreversible metabolic step, so it is an important point controlling entry of carbohydrate-derived carbon into acetyl-CoA metabolism.
Because one glucose produces two pyruvate molecules, PDH operates twice per glucose, yielding 2 acetyl-CoA, 2 CO₂, and 2 NADH.
The PDH complex itself contains three core enzyme activities, which we will introduce together with its required coenzymes on the next slide.

The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex is a multienzyme complex that requires five coenzymes to complete the conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA.
TLCFN : mnemonic The Lovely Coenzymes For Nerds  
TPP, derived from thiamine or vitamin B1, participates in the initial decarboxylation of pyruvate.
Lipoamide or lipoic acid acts as a flexible carrier within the complex, transferring both the acetyl group and reducing equivalents between enzyme components.
Coenzyme A, derived from vitamin B5, accepts the acetyl group to form acetyl-CoA.
FAD, derived from vitamin B2, participates in reoxidizing the reduced lipoamide arm.
Finally, NAD⁺, derived from vitamin B3, accepts electrons and is reduced to NADH.
The five-cofactor requirement explains why deficiencies affecting some B vitamins, especially thiamine, can impair oxidative metabolism.
Key point: PDH is not a single enzyme acting alone; it is a coordinated complex that depends on multiple cofactors to carry out oxidative decarboxylation.

Thiamine, or vitamin B1, is converted to thiamine pyrophosphate, TPP.
TPP is an essential cofactor for several oxidative decarboxylation reactions, including pyruvate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase. Therefore, thiamine deficiency impairs both the entry of pyruvate into acetyl-CoA metabolism and an important step within the TCA cycle itself.
When PDH activity falls, pyruvate cannot be efficiently converted to acetyl-CoA. More pyruvate is therefore available for conversion to lactate, which can contribute to hyperlactatemia and, in severe cases, lactic acidosis.
Reduced PDH and TCA activity also decrease ATP generation. Tissues with high energy requirements, particularly the brain, are therefore especially vulnerable.
Clinically, thiamine deficiency is important in patients with malnutrition or chronic alcohol use, and severe deficiency can cause Wernicke encephalopathy. 
n clinical practice, patients at risk of thiamine deficiency — especially those with chronic alcohol use, malnutrition, or prolonged poor intake — are generally given thiamine before or together with glucose. The reason is that glucose metabolism increases thiamine utilization, which may worsen the neurologic manifestations of Wernicke encephalopathy if thiamine stores are already depleted.

Pyruvate dehydrogenase is regulated mainly by reversible phosphorylation.
When PDH is phosphorylated, it is inactive. This phosphorylation is carried out by PDH kinase.
When the phosphate is removed by PDH phosphatase, PDH becomes active again.
A high-energy state, characterized by increased ATP, NADH, and acetyl-CoA, suppresses PDH activity. This prevents unnecessary oxidation of pyruvate when the cell already has adequate energy.
In contrast, when energy demand rises, ADP and NAD⁺ increase, favoring pyruvate oxidation.
In contracting muscle, increased Ca²⁺ activates PDH phosphatase, which activates PDH so that more acetyl-CoA can enter the TCA cycle and support ATP production.
Key point:PDH phosphorylation = OFFPDH dephosphorylation = ON

The TCA cycle, also called the citric acid cycle or Krebs cycle, occurs mainly in the mitochondrial matrix.
The cycle begins when a 2-carbon acetyl group from acetyl-CoA combines with 4-carbon oxaloacetate to form 6-carbon citrate.
As the cycle proceeds, the acetyl-derived carbon is oxidized and energy is captured primarily in reduced electron carriers:
3NADH + 1 FADH 2 + 1 GTP
and 2 CO₂ are released per turn.
The cycle ends by regenerating oxaloacetate, which can combine with another acetyl-CoA and begin another turn.
The TCA cycle itself produces only a small amount of direct high-energy phosphate as GTP. Most of its ATP yield comes later, when NADH and FADH₂ donate electrons to the electron transport chain.
Key point: the main role of the TCA cycle is to capture energy from acetyl-CoA in NADH and FADH₂, while regenerating oxaloacetate.

The TCA cycle consists of eight enzyme-catalyzed reactions.
The cycle begins when 2-carbon acetyl-CoA combines with 4-carbon oxaloacetate to produce 6-carbon citrate.
Two oxidative decarboxylation reactions then reduce the carbon number:
isocitrate, 6C → α-ketoglutarate, 5C
α-ketoglutarate, 5C → succinyl-CoA, 4C
These are the two steps where CO₂ is released.
Energy is captured at several points:
Step 3 produces NADH
Step 4 produces NADH
Step 5 produces GTP
Step 6 produces FADH₂
Step 8 produces NADH
At the end of Step 8, oxaloacetate is regenerated, allowing another acetyl-CoA to enter the cycle.
Students do not need to treat all eight reactions as equally important. We will focus next on the steps that are most important for regulation, energy capture, and clinical integration.

The first reaction of the TCA cycle is catalyzed by citrate synthase.
A 2-carbon acetyl group from acetyl-CoA combines with 4-carbon oxaloacetate, producing 6-carbon citrate.
2C+4C=6C 
This reaction is strongly favorable and is effectively irreversible under normal cellular conditions.
Citrate synthase activity depends heavily on whether its two substrates, acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate, are available. This is particularly important because acetyl-CoA cannot enter the cycle efficiently if oxaloacetate is depleted.
When citrate accumulates, this indicates that carbon and energy supply are relatively abundant. Citrate can therefore help reduce further metabolic flux, including inhibition of citrate synthase and inhibition of PFK-1 in glycolysis.
Key point: Acetyl-CoA cannot simply enter the TCA cycle alone; it must first combine with oxaloacetate to form citrate.

Isocitrate dehydrogenase catalyzes one of the most important regulatory reactions of the TCA cycle.
The enzyme converts 6-carbon isocitrate into 5-carbon α-ketoglutarate. During the reaction, one carbon is released as CO₂, and NAD⁺ is reduced to NADH.
This is therefore an oxidative decarboxylation reaction.
The enzyme responds to the cell’s energy status. When energy demand is high, ADP rises and stimulates the enzyme. In contracting muscle, increased Ca²⁺ also stimulates TCA-cycle activity so that ATP production can increase.
In contrast, abundant ATP and NADH signal that energy supply is already sufficient and inhibit the enzyme.
Key point: isocitrate dehydrogenase is a major flux-control point whose activity changes according to cellular energy demand.

α-Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase catalyzes the second oxidative decarboxylation of the TCA cycle:
alpha Ketoglutarate (5C)        →     Succinyl-CoA (4C)   +   CO2
At the same time, NAD⁺ is reduced to NADH.
This is an important flux-controlling step of the cycle. The enzyme responds to the cell’s energy state:
ADP activates α-KGDH, supporting greater TCA-cycle flux when energy demand is high.
Ca²⁺ activates the complex, particularly in contracting muscle.
ATP and NADH inhibit the enzyme when the cell is in a high-energy state.
Succinyl-CoA, the reaction product, also inhibits the complex by feedback/product inhibition.
Like PDH, α-KGDH is a multienzyme complex and uses the same five coenzymes: TPP, lipoamide, CoA, FAD, and NAD⁺.
Key point: α-KGDH helps regulate TCA-cycle flux by integrating low-energy signals (ADP, Ca²⁺) with high-energy/product signals (ATP, NADH, succinyl-CoA).

Succinyl-CoA synthetase converts 4-carbon succinyl-CoA into 4-carbon succinate.
The reaction uses energy stored in the high-energy thioester bond of succinyl-CoA to form GTP from GDP and inorganic phosphate.
Because GTP is formed directly from a metabolic intermediate, this is called substrate-level phosphorylation.
This is the only substrate-level phosphorylation reaction in the TCA cycle.
The distinction is important: GTP is generated directly here, whereas NADH and FADH₂ generate ATP later through oxidative phosphorylation.

The TCA cycle is regulated mainly at three important control points:
citrate synthase
isocitrate dehydrogenase
α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase
The overall principle is simple: when the cell needs more ATP, signals such as ADP and, in contracting muscle, Ca²⁺ increase cycle activity.
When energy is already abundant, ATP and NADH inhibit key enzymes and reduce TCA-cycle flux.
The cycle therefore responds continuously to the energy state of the cell rather than running at a fixed rate.

The TCA cycle does not contain a reaction in which oxygen is directly consumed.
Instead, oxygen is required at the level of the electron transport chain.
NADH and FADH₂ produced by the TCA cycle donate electrons to the ETC. Oxygen accepts those electrons at the end of the chain and is reduced to water.
This allows NAD⁺ and FAD to be regenerated.
If oxygen is severely limited, the ETC slows, NADH accumulates, and NAD⁺ becomes less available. Because several TCA-cycle reactions require NAD⁺, the cycle also slows.
Key point:No oxygen used directly in the TCA cycle; oxygen is required indirectly to keep the oxidized cofactors available.

The TCA cycle is described as amphibolic because it has both catabolic and anabolic functions.
Its catabolic role is to oxidize acetyl-CoA and capture energy in NADH, FADH₂, and GTP.
Its anabolic role is to provide intermediates for synthesis of other molecules. For example:
citrate can contribute to lipid synthesis
α-ketoglutarate can contribute to amino acid synthesis
succinyl-CoA contributes to heme synthesis
oxaloacetate can contribute to amino acid synthesis and gluconeogenesis
Because intermediates can leave the cycle for biosynthesis, the cell must also have mechanisms to replace them. That leads directly to the next topic: anaplerosis.

Pyruvate carboxylase is a mitochondrial enzyme that converts 3-carbon pyruvate into 4-carbon oxaloacetate.
The reaction requires ATP and biotin and adds one carbon in the form of CO₂.
Its main role in this context is anaplerotic: it replenishes oxaloacetate when TCA-cycle intermediates have been withdrawn for biosynthesis.
Oxaloacetate is also important for gluconeogenesis, so this reaction connects the TCA cycle with glucose production.
Pyruvate carboxylase is activated by acetyl-CoA. This makes metabolic sense because when acetyl-CoA accumulates, the cell needs sufficient oxaloacetate available to combine with it and sustain TCA-cycle activity.
Key distinction:PDH: pyruvate → acetyl-CoAPyruvate carboxylase: pyruvate → oxaloacetate

The TCA cycle is the central mitochondrial pathway that oxidizes acetyl-CoA while capturing energy mainly as NADH and FADH₂.
Its activity is regulated according to cellular energy demand, especially at citrate synthase, isocitrate dehydrogenase, and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.
The cycle is also amphibolic, because its intermediates are used in biosynthetic pathways. When those intermediates are removed, anaplerotic reactions replenish them, especially the conversion of pyruvate to oxaloacetate by pyruvate carboxylase.
Key point: the TCA cycle is not simply an energy-producing loop; it is a major metabolic hub connecting catabolism, biosynthesis, and cellular energy status.

This lecture focuses on how high-energy electrons from NADH and FADH₂ are transferred through the electron transport chain, how that transfer creates a proton gradient, and how ATP synthase converts the energy in that gradient into ATP.
Students should also understand why NADH and FADH₂ do not generate identical ATP yields, how inhibitors block oxidative phosphorylation, and how uncouplers allow electron transport to continue while ATP synthesis falls.

The TCA cycle does not produce most cellular ATP directly. Instead, it captures much of the energy from fuel oxidation in the reduced electron carriers NADH and FADH₂.
These carriers donate electrons to the electron transport chain, located in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
As electrons move through the ETC, some of the released energy is used to move protons from the mitochondrial matrix into the intermembrane space.
This creates a proton-motive force.
Protons then flow back into the matrix through ATP synthase, which uses this energy to produce ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate.
Oxygen is the final electron acceptor and is reduced to water.
Key point:TCA cycle → NADH/FADH₂ → ETC → proton gradient → ATP synthesis.

Redox reactions involve the transfer of electrons from one molecule to another.
A molecule that loses electrons is oxidized, while a molecule that gains electrons is reduced. Because electrons cannot simply disappear, oxidation and reduction always occur together.
In metabolism, NAD⁺ and FAD act as electron acceptors. When they gain electrons, they become NADH and FADH₂.
For example, during conversion of malate to oxaloacetate, malate is oxidized while NAD⁺ accepts electrons and is reduced to NADH.
The importance of this for oxidative phosphorylation is that NADH and FADH₂ deliver these electrons to the ETC, where their energy is used to drive proton pumping.
Key point:Fuel oxidation produces reduced carriers; the ETC reoxidizes those carriers and captures the released energy.

The electron transport chain is located in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
Electrons from NADH enter through Complex I, while electrons associated with succinate oxidation enter through Complex II. Both pathways converge at Coenzyme Q.
Electrons then pass through Complex III, cytochrome c, and Complex IV.
At Complex IV, oxygen accepts the electrons and is reduced to water.
The energy released during electron transfer is used by Complexes I, III, and IV to pump protons into the intermembrane space.
This creates the proton gradient that will later drive ATP synthesis.
Key point: Complex II transfers electrons but does not pump protons.

Complex I is the major entry point for electrons carried by NADH.
NADH is oxidized back to NAD⁺, allowing NAD⁺ to be reused in pathways such as the TCA cycle.
The two electrons pass through Complex I and are ultimately transferred to Coenzyme Q, reducing it to QH₂.
The energy released during this process is used to pump approximately 4 protons from the mitochondrial matrix into the intermembrane space.
This contributes to the electrochemical proton gradient that will later drive ATP synthesis.
Key point:NADH enters at Complex I; Complex I pumps H⁺ and transfers electrons to CoQ.

Complex II is succinate dehydrogenase, the same enzyme encountered in Step 6 of the TCA cycle.
It oxidizes succinate to fumarate. During this reaction, the enzyme’s tightly bound FAD is reduced, and the electrons are then transferred through Complex II to Coenzyme Q.
Unlike Complex I, Complex II does not pump protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane.
Therefore, electrons entering the ETC through Complex II generate a smaller proton gradient than electrons entering through Complex I.
Key point:Complex I pumps H⁺; Complex II does not.

The respiratory complexes do not physically pass electrons directly from one large complex to the next. Two smaller mobile carriers shuttle electrons between them.
Coenzyme Q, also called ubiquinone, is lipid-soluble and moves within the inner mitochondrial membrane. It accepts electrons from both Complex I and Complex II and transfers them to Complex III.
When CoQ accepts two electrons and two protons, it becomes ubiquinol, QH₂.
Cytochrome c is a small heme-containing protein located on the intermembrane-space side of the inner mitochondrial membrane. It transfers electrons from Complex III to Complex IV.
Unlike CoQ, cytochrome c transfers one electron at a time.
Key point:CoQ links I/II to III; cytochrome c links III to IV.

Complex III receives electrons from QH₂, the reduced form of Coenzyme Q.
As QH₂ is oxidized back to CoQ, its electrons pass through Complex III and are transferred to cytochrome c.
Cytochrome c carries one electron at a time from Complex III to Complex IV.
The transfer of a pair of electrons through Complex III results in the net movement of approximately 4 protons into the intermembrane space, contributing to the proton-motive force.
Key point:Complex III connects CoQ to cytochrome c and helps build the proton gradient.

Complex IV, also called cytochrome c oxidase, is the final complex of the electron transport chain.
It accepts electrons from cytochrome c and transfers them to molecular oxygen, which is the final electron acceptor.
Oxygen combines with electrons and protons to form water.
Complex IV also pumps protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space, contributing to the proton-motive force.
Per two electrons transferred, approximately 2 protons are pumped across the membrane. PubMed Central (PMC)
Key point:Electron transport ends at Complex IV, where oxygen is reduced to water.

Electron transfer through the respiratory chain releases energy.
Complexes I, III, and IV use this energy to move protons from the mitochondrial matrix into the intermembrane space. Complex II transfers electrons but does not pump protons.
This creates two differences across the inner mitochondrial membrane:
a concentration gradient, because more H⁺ accumulates outside the matrix
an electrical gradient, because the intermembrane-space side becomes relatively more positive
Together these constitute the proton-motive force.
The proton-motive force is stored energy. The next step is to convert this stored energy into ATP through ATP synthase.
Key point:The ETC itself does not directly make ATP; it first stores energy as a proton-motive force.

The respiratory chain first stores energy as a proton-motive force across the inner mitochondrial membrane.
ATP synthase then allows protons to move back into the matrix in a controlled way.
The F₀ portion spans the membrane and conducts protons. Proton flow drives rotation within the enzyme.
The F₁ portion faces the matrix and contains the catalytic sites that synthesize ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate.
This mechanism is called chemiosmosis.
Key distinction: the ETC and ATP synthase perform different jobs:
ETC: builds the proton gradientATP synthase: uses the proton gradient to make ATP.

The ATP yield from NADH and FAD-linked electrons differs because they enter the respiratory chain at different points.
NADH enters at Complex I, so its electrons pass through three proton-pumping complexes: I, III, and IV.
Electrons from succinate oxidation enter through Complex II, which does not pump protons. Therefore, they only contribute to proton pumping at Complexes III and IV.
As a result, the approximate ATP yields are:
NADH: ~2.5 ATP
FADH₂-linked electrons: ~1.5 ATP
Key point:The difference is not because one carrier has “more energetic electrons” in a vague sense; it is because the electrons enter the chain at different positions and therefore drive different amounts of proton pumping.

Oxidative phosphorylation consists of two linked processes.
First, the electron transport chain transfers electrons from NADH and FAD-linked carriers to oxygen. The energy released during this transfer is used to pump protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane.
Second, the resulting proton-motive force drives protons back through ATP synthase, which converts ADP and inorganic phosphate into ATP.
Oxygen is essential because it accepts the electrons at the end of the chain.
Key point: the ETC does not directly synthesize ATP; it creates the proton gradient that ATP synthase uses to make ATP.

Why Do We Need Oxygen?
Oxygen is the final electron acceptor at Complex IV, where it is reduced to water.
This allows the ETC to continue pumping H⁺ and maintaining the proton gradient needed for ATP synthesis.
When oxygen is unavailable:
Electron transport and proton pumping stop.
ATP production falls sharply.
Cells rely more on anaerobic glycolysis, increasing lactate production.
Severe oxygen deprivation can cause lactic acidosis, cellular injury, and organ failure.
The brain and heart are particularly vulnerable because of their high ATP requirements.
Take-home message: Oxygen is essential for sustained mitochondrial ATP production. Without it, cells cannot maintain normal energy production and function.

ETC inhibitors impair oxidative phosphorylation by blocking electron transfer through the respiratory chain or by preventing proton flow through ATP synthase. The main consequences are reduced electron flow, reduced oxygen consumption, loss of the proton gradient, and decreased ATP synthesis. Your original lecture emphasizes the same overall effects of ETC inhibition. 18. Electron Transport Chain
Cyanide is the key clinical example. It inhibits Complex IV, cytochrome c oxidase, so electrons can no longer be transferred efficiently to oxygen. As oxidative phosphorylation fails, ATP production falls and cells rely more heavily on glycolysis, which can contribute to lactic acidosis. The original lecture also links cyanide-mediated Complex IV inhibition with reduced ATP production and lactic acidosis. 18. Electron Transport Chain
A major current treatment for cyanide poisoning is hydroxocobalamin, which binds cyanide and facilitates its detoxification.
Carbon monoxide can also inhibit Complex IV, but its major clinical effect is usually due to binding hemoglobin and forming carboxyhemoglobin, which reduces oxygen delivery to tissues. Mitochondrial inhibition can contribute, especially at high exposure.
Key distinction: ETC inhibitors reduce oxidative phosphorylation by blocking the chain or ATP synthase. This is different from uncouplers, where electron transport can continue but the proton gradient is dissipated and ATP production falls.

Uncoupling means that electron transport continues, but ATP synthesis is no longer efficiently linked to it.
Normally, the ETC pumps protons from the mitochondrial matrix into the intermembrane space, creating a proton gradient. Protons then return through ATP synthase, and that energy is used to make ATP.
With an uncoupler, protons return to the matrix without passing through ATP synthase. As a result, the proton gradient is dissipated.
The major consequences are:
electron transport increases, because the ETC tries to restore the proton gradient
oxygen consumption increases
the proton gradient decreases
ATP synthesis decreases
more of the energy from fuel oxidation is released as heat
This is the key difference from an ETC inhibitor. An inhibitor slows electron transport and oxygen consumption, whereas an uncoupler can increase both while still reducing ATP synthesis.
DNP, 2,4-dinitrophenol, is a toxic chemical uncoupler. It carries protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane and dissipates the proton gradient. This can markedly increase heat production and may cause severe hyperthermia. Your original lecture identifies DNP as a toxic uncoupler that was historically used for weight loss. 18. Electron Transport Chain
Aspirin overdose can also produce uncoupling. Aspirin is converted to salicylate, and at toxic concentrations salicylate can uncouple oxidative phosphorylation. This contributes to increased metabolic rate and heat production and is part of the metabolic disturbance seen in salicylate toxicity.
Thermogenin, UCP1, is a physiological uncoupler found in brown adipose tissue. It allows controlled proton leak back into the matrix, so the energy of the proton gradient is released as heat rather than captured as ATP. This is important for non-shivering thermogenesis, particularly in newborns. Your uploaded lecture makes this same connection between UCP1, brown adipose tissue, and heat generation. 18. Electron Transport Chain
Key point: uncoupling can be pathological, as with DNP or salicylate toxicity, or physiological, as with UCP1-mediated thermogenesis.

This slide integrates the whole lecture.
NADH donates electrons through Complex I, while electrons from succinate enter through Complex II. Both pathways converge at CoQ and continue through Complex III, cytochrome c, and Complex IV, where oxygen acts as the final electron acceptor.
Complexes I, III, and IV pump protons, creating the proton-motive force. ATP synthase then uses this stored energy to synthesize ATP.
ETC inhibitors reduce electron transport and oxygen consumption. Uncouplers behave differently: they dissipate the proton gradient, so electron transport and oxygen consumption can increase even though ATP synthesis falls.

This lecture focuses on how the body maintains blood glucose when dietary glucose becomes unavailable.
Gluconeogenesis synthesizes glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors, particularly lactate, glycerol, and glucogenic amino acids. It occurs mainly in the liver, with an increasing contribution from the kidney during prolonged fasting.
We will examine why gluconeogenesis cannot simply be glycolysis running backwards, how the three irreversible glycolytic reactions are bypassed, and how the pathway is reciprocally regulated with glycolysis.
We will also connect the pathway to physiological processes such as the Cori cycle and glucose–alanine cycle, and to clinically relevant regulation of hepatic glucose production.

After a meal, circulating glucose is supplied mainly by absorption from the gastrointestinal tract.
As dietary glucose disappears, the liver initially maintains blood glucose largely through glycogenolysis.
As fasting continues and hepatic glycogen stores fall, gluconeogenesis increases and becomes progressively more important.
The main gluconeogenic organ is the liver, although the kidney contributes increasingly during prolonged fasting.
The hormonal pattern of fasting is characterized by lower insulin and higher glucagon, which favors hepatic glucose production.

The pathways that maintain blood glucose do not switch on and off abruptly.
Dietary glucose, glycogenolysis, and gluconeogenesis can overlap, but their relative contributions change with time after the last meal.
Soon after eating, dietary glucose is the major source of blood glucose.
As dietary glucose falls, hepatic glycogenolysis increases and becomes more important.
At the same time, gluconeogenesis is already occurring and gradually increases as fasting continues.
As liver glycogen stores become depleted, the contribution from glycogenolysis falls and gluconeogenesis becomes the dominant source of blood glucose.
Therefore, the transition from one glucose source to another is gradual and overlapping, not a series of discrete stages.
Key point:All of these processes can occur at the same time; fasting mainly changes the rate and relative contribution of each pathway to maintaining blood glucose.

Gluconeogenesis is an anabolic, energy-requiring pathway that produces glucose from compounds that are not carbohydrates.
It becomes increasingly important when dietary glucose is unavailable, particularly during fasting.
The liver is the major gluconeogenic organ, while the kidney contributes increasingly during prolonged fasting.
The pathway spans more than one cellular compartment. Some reactions occur in the mitochondrial matrix, whereas most occur in the cytosol. The exact route depends partly on the starting substrate.
The major substrates introduced in this lecture are lactate, glycerol, pyruvate, and glucogenic amino acids. The original lecture also lists propionate as a gluconeogenic substrate.

The body can synthesize glucose from several non-carbohydrate precursors.
Lactate is produced continuously by red blood cells and can also be produced by exercising skeletal muscle. It is transported to the liver, converted back to pyruvate, and used for gluconeogenesis. This relationship forms the basis of the Cori cycle.
Glycerol is released when triglycerides are broken down in adipose tissue. It enters gluconeogenesis through the triose-phosphate pathway.
Glucogenic amino acids, particularly alanine, provide carbon skeletons that can enter gluconeogenesis. 
Alanine is a major glucogenic amino acid because muscle converts pyruvate to alanine and sends it to the liver, where it is converted back to pyruvate for gluconeogenesis.
Pyruvate itself can enter the gluconeogenic pathway directly.

most fatty acids, especially even-chain fatty acids, do not provide net glucose.
Their β-oxidation generates acetyl-CoA, which enters the TCA cycle, but there is no net conversion of acetyl-CoA carbon into glucose.
An important exception is odd-chain fatty acids, which produce propionyl-CoA. 
Also, the glycerol backbone of triglycerides can enter gluconeogenesis.

Gluconeogenesis requires energy because glucose synthesis from non-carbohydrate precursors involves several energetically demanding steps.
During fasting, adipose tissue breaks down triglycerides and releases fatty acids into the blood.
The liver oxidizes these fatty acids by β-oxidation, generating energy that supports gluconeogenesis. The uploaded lecture also emphasizes that β-oxidation generates acetyl-CoA, which activates pyruvate carboxylase, an important early enzyme in the gluconeogenic pathway. 
This creates an important metabolic link: while most fatty-acid carbon does not become glucose directly, fatty-acid oxidation helps make gluconeogenesis possible.

During anaerobic glycolysis, skeletal muscle can produce lactate. Red blood cells also continuously produce lactate because they depend on glycolysis.
Lactate enters the circulation and travels to the liver.
In the liver, lactate is converted back to pyruvate and then to glucose through gluconeogenesis. The glucose can then return to the blood and be reused by muscle or other glucose-dependent tissues.
The Cori cycle therefore allows peripheral tissues to continue glycolysis while the liver performs the energy-consuming task of regenerating glucose.

Alanine is an important glucogenic amino acid.
In skeletal muscle, amino groups generated during amino-acid metabolism can be transferred to pyruvate to form alanine. Alanine then travels through the blood to the liver.
In the liver, alanine is converted back to pyruvate. The pyruvate can then enter gluconeogenesis and be converted to glucose.
The glucose is released into the circulation and can return to skeletal muscle.
An important difference from the Cori cycle is that the glucose–alanine cycle also transports nitrogen from muscle to liver, not just carbon.

Gluconeogenesis is not simply glycolysis running backward.
Most glycolytic reactions are near equilibrium and can operate in either direction depending on substrate and product concentrations.
However, three glycolytic reactions are strongly favorable in the forward direction and are therefore effectively irreversible under cellular conditions:
hexokinase/glucokinase
phosphofructokinase-1
pyruvate kinase
These reactions must be bypassed by different enzymes during gluconeogenesis.
The first irreversible glycolytic step, catalyzed by pyruvate kinase, requires two gluconeogenic reactions to bypass it, which is why three irreversible glycolytic steps require four alternative gluconeogenic reactions overall.

The Three Bypasses of Gluconeogenesis:
Gluconeogenesis uses most of the reversible reactions of glycolysis in the opposite direction.
The three essentially irreversible glycolytic steps cannot simply run backward, so they require bypass reactions. 
Bypass 1: Pyruvate → PEP 
Pyruvate carboxylase: pyruvate → oxaloacetate 
PEP carboxykinase (PEPCK): oxaloacetate → PEP
Bypass 2: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate → fructose-6-phosphate 
Enzyme: fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase
Bypass 3: Glucose-6-phosphate → glucose 
Enzyme: glucose-6-phosphatase
Therefore, three irreversible glycolytic steps are bypassed using four gluconeogenic enzymes. 
Key point: The first bypass requires two enzymes, which is why there are four gluconeogenic bypass enzymes in total.

Pyruvate kinase catalyzes an irreversible glycolytic step, so gluconeogenesis cannot simply convert pyruvate directly back to PEP.
Pyruvate first enters the mitochondrion.
Pyruvate carboxylase converts pyruvate to oxaloacetate.
This reaction requires ATP, biotin, and CO₂ and is activated by acetyl-CoA. 
Oxaloacetate is then converted to PEP by PEP carboxykinase (PEPCK).
oxaloacetate cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane directly. It is converted to malate or aspartate, transported to the cytosol, and then regenerated as oxaloacetate.

Acetyl-CoA Activates Pyruvate Carboxylase:
Pyruvate carboxylase is a mitochondrial enzyme that converts pyruvate to oxaloacetate.
This reaction requires ATP, bicarbonate (CO₂ source), and biotin.
Acetyl-CoA is an obligate activator of pyruvate carboxylase; without it, enzyme activity is very low. 
During fasting, fatty-acid β-oxidation increases, producing more acetyl-CoA in liver mitochondria.
High acetyl-CoA therefore promotes Pyruvate →Oxaloacetate and supports gluconeogenesis.
This links fatty-acid oxidation to glucose production during fasting.
Key point: High acetyl-CoA signals that fatty acids are being used for energy and helps direct pyruvate toward gluconeogenesis.

Pyruvate can either be oxidized to acetyl-CoA by pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) or enter gluconeogenesis through pyruvate carboxylase.
High acetyl-CoA:
inhibits PDH
activates pyruvate carboxylase
This diverts pyruvate away from further oxidation and toward oxaloacetate formation and gluconeogenesis. 
This is an example of coordinate regulation, where one metabolic signal controls two competing pathways in opposite directions.
Key message:High acetyl-CoA redirects pyruvate from oxidation toward gluconeogenesis.

PFK-1 catalyzes an essentially irreversible glycolytic reaction.
Therefore, gluconeogenesis uses a different enzyme: fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase.
It removes a phosphate from fructose-1,6-bisphosphate to form fructose-6-phosphate.
This is one of the major regulatory steps of gluconeogenesis.
Its activity is coordinated with PFK-1 so that glycolysis and gluconeogenesis are not strongly active at the same time.

Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate is an important regulator of the balance between glycolysis and gluconeogenesis.
High insulin increases F-2,6-BP.
High F-2,6-BP activates PFK-1 and inhibits fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase, favoring glycolysis.
High glucagon lowers F-2,6-BP.
Low F-2,6-BP reduces PFK-1 activity and allows fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase to act, favoring gluconeogenesis. 
This is an example of reciprocal regulation: when one pathway is favored, the opposing pathway is suppressed.
Key message:High F-2,6-BP favors glycolysis; low F-2,6-BP favors gluconeogenesis.

PFK-2 and FBPase-2 are two activities of the same bifunctional enzyme.
In liver, insulin promotes dephosphorylation, activating PFK-2 and increasing F-2,6-BP.
Glucagon increases cAMP and PKA activity, causing phosphorylation of the bifunctional enzyme.
In the phosphorylated state, FBPase-2 activity predominates, F-2,6-BP falls, and gluconeogenesis is favored.

Glucose-6-phosphate is the final phosphorylated intermediate before free glucose is formed.
Glucose-6-phosphatase removes the phosphate group.
Free glucose can then leave the cell and enter the blood.
The enzyme is present in liver and kidney, but not skeletal muscle. 19. Gluconeogenesis
This is why skeletal muscle glycogen is used for the muscle’s own energy needs rather than directly maintaining blood glucose.

During fasting, blood glucose falls and glucagon rises.
Glucagon activates the cAMP/PKA pathway in the liver.
This lowers fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, which:
decreases glycolysis
favors gluconeogenesis
Glucagon also decreases hepatic pyruvate kinase activity, helping preserve PEP for gluconeogenesis. 
At the same time, adipose tissue releases fatty acids, which undergo β-oxidation in the liver.
Fatty-acid oxidation:
provides ATP needed for gluconeogenesis
increases acetyl-CoA
Acetyl-CoA activates pyruvate carboxylase, promoting formation of oxaloacetate and supporting gluconeogenesis. 19. Gluconeogenesis
These hormonal and metabolic changes act together to increase hepatic glucose production and maintain blood glucose during fasting.
Key point: During fasting, glucagon reduces glycolysis, while fatty-acid oxidation supplies the energy and acetyl-CoA that support gluconeogenesis.

Metformin is a medication used in type 2 diabetes.
One of its important metabolic effects is inhibition of hepatic gluconeogenesis. 
This decreases hepatic glucose production and helps lower blood glucose.
This clinical example shows why regulation of gluconeogenesis is important in disease as well as fasting physiology.
